To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

‘In two subjects with ragweed‐induced asthma, allergen‐inducible increase in airway hyper‐responsiveness occurred only after repeated allergens inhalations, and this was associated with a small, equivocal late response.’
allergen inhalation in two subjects with ragweed‐induced asthma resulted in allergen‐inducible increase in airway reactivity only after repeated allergens inhalations.
the allergen‐induce increase in airway reactivity may be a consequence of repeated allergen exposure, and not a consequence of the first allergen inhalation.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of allergen inhalation on airway responsiveness to histamine and methacholine in subjects with allergic asthma and rhinitis, and with the role of histamine in the pathogenesis and treatment of allergic asthma.
the mechanisms of allergen‐ and exercise‐induced asthma.
the mechanisms by which allergen exposure leads to the late phase response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
‘the allergen‐inducible increase in responsiveness is an important feature of the allergic asthmatic subject’ and that ‘it is not a feature of the allergic rhinitis patient’.
allergen‐induce increases in airway reactivity are seen in only some asthmatic subjects, and that the prevalence of this response in naturally occurring asthma is unknown.
allergen challenge may induce ‘priming’ in some subjects, and that such an effect may be important in naturally occurring allergic asthma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the allergen‐inducible late sequelae in the two subjects studied were not associated with an immediate increase in airway hyperresponsiveness, and the allergen‐associated increase in airway reactivity occurred only after the second and subsequent inhalations.
allergen challenge studies in allergic subjects with asthma and rhinitis may be complicated by a priming phenomenon.
we have shown that the late response is a separate phenomenon from the immediate response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
repeated exposure to the allergen is necessary for the allergen to cause an increase in airway hyperresponsiveness.
allergen inhalation can cause an increase in airway hyper‐responsiveness, which may not be apparent until the second or third allergen challenge.
the effect of allergen inhalation on airway responsiveness is not necessarily the same after every inhalation, and that it is not necessarily associated with a late reaction.
